## Overview

Use a classification forest to predict class labels and probabilities from
numeric and categorical predictors. We simulate a binary response, fit on 80
observations, and evaluate predictions on 20 held-out observations.

## Prerequisites

Follow [Get Started](get-started.html) to install RLT, then load the package:

```{r load-package}
library(RLT)
```

## Data Preparation

The first five predictors are numeric and the last five are factors. Factor
columns tell RLT to use categorical splits. The probability of class `1`
increases with the first numeric predictor; the other predictors have no effect
on the simulated response. The response itself must be a factor for
classification.

```{r data-prep}
set.seed(1)

trainn <- 80
testn  <- 20
n <- trainn + testn
p <- 10

# Continuous + categorical predictors (last half as factors)
X1 <- matrix(rnorm(n * (p/2)), n, p/2)
X2 <- matrix(as.integer(runif(n * (p/2)) * 10), n, p/2)  # integers 0-9

X <- data.frame(X1, X2)
X[, (p/2 + 1):p] <- lapply(X[, (p/2 + 1):p], as.factor)

# Binary outcome via a simple logistic signal
prob  <- plogis(-0.5 + 2 * X[, 1])
y     <- factor(rbinom(n, 1, prob = prob), levels = c(0, 1))

# Train / test split
trainX <- X[1:trainn, ]
trainY <- y[1:trainn]
testX  <- X[(trainn + 1):(trainn + testn), ]
testY  <- y[(trainn + 1):(trainn + testn)]
```

## Fit a classification model

We use 200 trees and sample half of the predictors as split candidates at each
node with `mtry = p/2`. Setting `nsplit = 0` searches all available cutpoints for
numeric candidates. The explicit `seed` controls fitting randomness; see
[Random Seed and Reproducibility](feature-seed.html) for the distinction from
`set.seed()` used for data generation above.

```{r fit-model}
fit <- RLT(
  trainX, trainY, model = "classification",
  ntrees = 200, mtry = p/2, nsplit = 0,
  seed = 1, ncores = 1, verbose = FALSE
)
```

## Predict

```{r predict}
pred <- predict(fit, testX)
head(data.frame(Observed = testY, Predicted = pred$Prediction))
head(pred$Prob)
```

`pred$Prediction` already contains factor class labels. `pred$Prob` contains one
row per held-out observation and one column per class, in `levels(trainY)` order.

## Evaluate

The fitted object's `Prediction` component contains out-of-bag (OOB) class
predictions. Each training observation is classified using only trees whose
resample omitted it. The test predictions use the fitted forest on observations
reserved before fitting.

```{r evaluate}
list(
  OOB_Accuracy = round(mean(fit$Prediction == trainY), 4),
  Test_Accuracy = round(mean(pred$Prediction == testY), 4)
)
```

Accuracy is the fraction of correctly classified observations, so larger
values indicate better classification. OOB accuracy uses the training
observations without including them in the corresponding trees; test accuracy
uses the 20 held-out observations. With this small test set, each additional
correct classification changes test accuracy by 0.05.

## Inspect the fitted object

```{r inspect}
print(fit)
```

The printed summary records the forest settings and OOB misclassification
error, which is one minus OOB accuracy. To assess which predictors the forest
relies on, continue to [Variable Importance](variable-importance.html).
